of what the body and the emotional body want to do, which was release it. And I had to discount
any of this justification of the milk and for foaming and I just go, you know,
really this isn't about that. So this is another reason to just wait on the whole explanation,
justification, trying to understand why we feel what we feel. Because in this case,
obviously my anger and rage had nothing to do with hot chocolate. It was something else.
And you may never know what.
In this case, I didn't know what.
I had stored it up from who knows where and who knows when.
And we'll talk about some of those reasons possibly in another audio.
The important thing was, what do you do about it?
You breathe it, you release it, you let it go.
And what I did in those cases, I just limited my interactions with other people
during those days where I was really toxic.
And stuff was oozing out my pores and my cells.
Until I felt better.
So this is what can happen in an emotional release process.
Sometimes we can let it go in a few breaths and we notice a difference.
And sometimes we'll do it for 20 minutes and we'll be a little different or a lot different.
And sometimes we've started to release this pent-up energy.
And this is particularly further along in a process, typically.
You might find the larger pools to be released.
In the beginning, it'll be smaller.
Later on, you might go through a phase where there's a couple big pools to let go of.
As you become comfortable releasing emotions and you feel safe in the process,
the body goes, hey, we've got this big thing we want to let go of
that we've just been holding because we haven't been really safe,
feeling safe about our emotions.
And then it opens up like it was for me with grief or anger.
And at that point, it really doesn't matter why.
The important thing is do the cleansing, do the healing,
do the release so you aren't carrying it around anymore.
Hope this is helpful.
Eventually, I may do a whole course on emotions,
but for now, I want to do this one exercise
and get it out and make it available
because it's just very simple and very useful.
Hope you find it helpful.
This audio is on releasing emotions,
emotional release using breath work.
The do's and don'ts.
This is Gary Van Wormerdam from PathwayToHappiness.com.
Good luck.
Happy hunting.

09 Emotions Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/09-emotions/09-emotions-transcript

                                                                        May 11, 2019

Today’s topic is the emotions. Something I would have loved to have gotten to earlier,
but there was other stuff more pressing that we needed to address first. What I want to
share with you today is a huge topic. The topic today is about the emotions and what I’ll
call the emotional body. That emotional body is that vehicle of perception that we have
that allows us to perceive emotions.

We have a physical body and that physical body allows us through our skin to sense
textures and temperature of what we’re touching. Our emotional body works very much
the same way. It allows us to sense the emotion that is there. The same way our physical
body can experience temperature. I want you to think of your emotional body really just
as a sensory device, a means of perception.

The way I want to begin is with an exercise. For this exercise you’ll need to be sitting
still, preferably with your eyes closed. What I want you to do is, just for starters, to focus
on your breath, relax, take a couple of deep breaths. Let every thought of the day, idea,
the week, whatever that has been going on, let it dissolve. I want you to think of some
kind of unpleasant emotion and uncomfortable emotion, fear, or anger, or sadness, or
guilt. I want you to create that emotion. You may need to draw on a story or the past,
where you had an incident where you felt that emotion. Go ahead and think of an
instance in the past where you felt that emotion that was unpleasant, and use that
memory to create that unpleasant emotion and allow yourself to create that unpleasant
emotion. Just feel it. Once you have the emotion, perhaps you can dissolve the memory.
Let go the story that you used to get yourself there. Just notice, you just feel the
emotion. Then what I want you to do is dissolve the emotion.

Just dissolve the emotion, put your attention back on your breath. Be present in the
moment. Notice what is right here right now. Notice how that shifts what you feel
emotionally. And let everything return to a neutral, the emotional neutral. Once you’re
there, what I want you to do is think of a very pleasant, wonderful, enjoyable emotion.
Maybe something that is related to a memory of a past event, or something upcoming
that you’re excited about. Use that story, or that memory if you will, but create within
yourself that wonderful emotion, whether it’ll be love, or gratitude, excitement.
Whatever that joy is just create that emotion. Enjoy the memory or story that goes with
it. Make it as strong and as intense as you can. Let that emotion fill up your whole body.
Even then, let go of the story of that emotion with your attention just on the emotion
itself, without it needing to be related to anything. Then go ahead and dissolve the
emotion just by returning your attention to your breath, be here in the present moment.





                                                                                                                           1/10

Being present with what your physical body is, sitting and doing right now. Let your
emotional body return to neutral. Once it’s at neutral, what I’d like you to do, pick
another emotion within the unpleasant spectrum of emotion, anger and guilt, or
frustration and create that emotion. Use a story if you need to. Use a memory, go back
to a memory, whatever is in your arsenal of stories and memories and experiences. Go
ahead, use them. Create an unpleasant emotion. Let it become as intense as you care to.
Let go the story about it, if you used one. Notice that you can have emotion without
having a story or idea. Then dissolve the emotion.

Returning your attention to your breath. Returning your awareness to what your
physical body is just doing right now. Bringing your attention away from the memory
and the story. Letting your whole physical and emotional system return to neutral. Once
you’re at neutral, I want you to pick another emotion on the pleasant end of the
spectrum. An enjoyable emotion, something in the realm of feeling love. Pick that
emotion and then create it in your emotional body. Let it expand, make it grow bigger.
Use a memory, or a story, or an event to make it bigger, if it works for you. Make that
pleasant and enjoyable emotion as big as possible, as intense as possible. Then let go of
the story that you used to create it, and notice you can just have the emotion without a
story. Just put your attention on the emotion. Enjoy the love you feel and know that you
can have that without any story. Then at this point, let that emotion dissolve. Turn your
attention to your breath. Put your attention on what your physical body is feeling right
now. Let your emotional body go to neutral or drift towards neutral.

You can open your eyes. The reason I do this exercise is for you to have the experience
that the emotions are things that you can create. Emotions do not necessarily get
created by reaction or because of outside events. If we remember back to our abdication
of power exercise, we told a lot of stories and we attributed a lot of outside factors
through those stories to what made us have a reaction. In this exercise, we get to see
that we can create our own emotions just from our own will. We may not be very
practiced at this point, so we still may need at times to use a story to get us there, but we
can still get ourselves there. That gratitude exercise is just that kind of exercise that will
teach us and help us exercise the muscle, so that we are stronger and stronger and more
proficient at putting ourselves in an emotional state that we choose. With practice we
become more proficient at keeping ourselves there.

I doubt anybody has ever told you in your life that you experience the emotions that you
create. You will experience the emotions that you create. That you are the creator of
those emotions, consciously or unconsciously. That you can consciously create any
emotion that you choose. Understanding this point can have a profound impact on your
life. Just knowing that you can pick an emotion and create it, is extraordinary. No one
ever told me that that’s how you became happy. It took me a while to figure out that I
could create my own happiness. I didn’t have to be dependent on anybody else to do it.
With the creation of that emotion, now was a function of my will and my intent. That
took some mastering and getting a hold of this skill.



                                                                                                                           2/10

What I’m asking you to realize is that emotion is a result. It’s a result of your intent to
create. It may have been the result of how you create through a story. You may have
went into a story and used a story to create the emotion, we use our intent to create the
story and a by-product of the story is the emotion. My experience is that emotions are
largely just an experience of feedback.

Going back to the emotional body. If we look at the physical body and we touch
something that’s cold, we will say that that temperature is just the sensation that we feel.
But why do we feel something cold? We feel it because we’ve put our hand on it. If we
touch something hot and we burn our hand, that is just the feedback that we’re getting,
telling us what temperature of that object is.

Same thing with emotions, but emotions don’t get created by tactile touch. If we believe
in the story about ourselves that we are ugly, or that we are unworthy, or that we’re
stupid, we create that story about ourselves. With our belief in it we get the feeling of
being unworthy, we get the feeling of being stupid. If at another time during the week
we do something successful and we feel great about ourselves, we think we are fabulous,
we believe that story about ourselves and the emotion we get is feeling fabulous. Or
whatever that word is. It’s ecstatic, it’s joyful, it’s self-love. We get that emotion, because
we’re believing in a story that produces that result. The emotion is a by-product of
believing in that story.

If we believe judgmental, self-critical thoughts, we get the corresponding emotional
feeling. If we believe wonderful, lofty, beautiful ideas of ourselves, we get the
corresponding emotion. One of the big mistakes we make is that we then use the
emotion that we feel as evidence. Take for example that something didn’t go well. We
think we’re failure and somebody asks us “How do you feel?” Since I feel like a failure,
that feeling is something we interpret as some kind of proof. We feel like a failure, we
believe we’re failure. But the reason we feel like a failure is because we already believe it.
We create this spiraling move. We believe we’re failure, and because we believe it, we get
the feeling of unworthiness. Then that brings us down a notch, and it feels like that
belief is now true. We have the emotional support to that story. We start to use that
feeling as evidence that the story is true.

People ask “How do we know we’re a failure?” I can feel it. If we believe we’re not
lovable, then no matter how many people love us, we don’t feel lovable. We have the
emotional experience to support that story. Of course, the emotional experience is
created from that story, but we don’t notice that. Pretty much for any story that we
believe, we create emotional response that corresponds to that story being true. That
story is true only for us. We have the experience of it being true, because we believe it.
This is how we create the emotions we create. We believe our stories and our emotional
body says “Okay. We will give you feedback for whatever you believe.” Having that story
that nobody loves us, we’re unworthy or whatever the story is, we’re a failure.





                                                                                                                           3/10

That story, believing that story is like a splinter in our mind. It’s causing pain. Well, if
we have a splinter in our physical body, that splinter causes pain. The pain it causes is
not the problem. We could say that there’s this splinter, and then there’s the result of
having this splinter there, which is the physical pain. To stop the pain we don’t have to
deaden it and take painkillers. No. What we really need done is to remove the splinter.
That pain is actually a great feedback mechanism saying “There’s something wrong
here. You need to look at this part of your body, because it has a splinter. Go take it
out.” That pain is a great feedback telling us something is not working here.

When we have a story in our mind that we’re not worthy, we’re a failure, we get a
corresponding painful emotion. The painful unpleasant feeling is not the problem. It’s
the aspect we notice. But it’s not the problem. It’s just pointing at a story that is saying
“I’m unworthy. I’m a failure. I’m a loser.” That story is the real cause of the pain. It’s the
splinter. The emotion is just a flag to us saying “Hey, there’s a lie here that needs to be
removed.” That painful emotion is helping us to point out the lies in our life. But the real
picture what I want us to understand here is, that emotional body is giving feedback for
what’s going on.

If we touch a hot stove and our hand is burning, we’re in pain. The problem is not the
pain. The pain is a very healthy feedback to tell us our flesh is in trouble. The solution is
to take our hand off the stove, not to try and make the pain go away. That’s common
sense. What we too often do in our life is when we feel something painful emotionally, is
we try and stop the emotion, but we don’t look at what the painful emotion is being
caused by. Where is the real splinter? Where’s the real story we’re buying into? Too
often we try to repress the emotion or we judge it, or we say “Gosh, I wish I didn’t feel
this. I shouldn’t feel this way” and we push it down. But that emotion is just a natural
result of believing whatever story we’re believing.

If we look at our emotions as this kind of feedback mechanism, we don’t need to push
them away. If we get angry, so often we judge ourselves “I wish I hadn’t gotten so angry.
I was really out of line. I hate it when I do that.” That’s a very self-critical judgement of
ourselves, based on the emotion we feel. But the emotion we feel is just an effect of root
cause. That root cause is the story we bought into about why we got angry? The reason I
say this is to give you this clarity, so we can stop judging our emotion. Our emotions are
just our emotions. If we’re emotionally in pain, the emotion isn’t the problem. It’s just
the result of some cause. Let’s look at the cause and stop blaming our emotions for
being there.

If we understand this point of view, then even anger isn’t such a bad emotion. Anger is
just a result of believing a story that makes us angry. Guilt, the emotion of guilt, is not
the problem. The story we buy into that brings about guilt that can go. But let’s make
sure that we don’t blame the feeling. The feeling of guilt is a perfectly natural response if
we’re going to believe that kind of lie about ourselves. Let’s not spend time wishing we
weren’t guilty, because that’s a judgment on our emotions. Thank God we notice we’re




                                                                                                                           4/10

guilty, because that’s going to indicate us some lie story that we’ve bought into. Feeling
guilty isn’t bad. You notice when we feel guilty is a great gift for us to go find and
dissolve this lie that we’ve bought into.

I want to introduce to you one other way that emotions are created. And that is,
emotions are created as a natural response, a sensory response to what we perceive. If
we perceive something beautiful and we often say “Oh, it took my breath away.” Maybe
we don’t say it often enough. But we say something like “Oh, it took my breath away.”
Well, it didn’t take our breath away. What it took away was our mind. It took away our
interpretation and it made our mind very quiet. What happened is, we perceived that
person or that scenery just purely as it is, with such beauty and our emotional body
responded to perceiving that as it is. This is the emotional body responding to pure
perception. Even feeling things physically, creates a perception that we respond to
emotionally.

If we hear music, we can respond to emotionally, not necessarily because it triggers a
memory, but music we’ve never heard before, the beauty of it, can elicit emotion. What
we touch, what we smell, what we taste, everything that we perceive can elicit an
emotional response. If we have something frightening, we’re walking in the woods, a
bear or a snake comes to our attention. We can go to fear, and it’s strictly intrinsic
authentic fight-or-flight syndrome. The same way that we have our emotional response
to something beautiful, we can have our emotional response to something that’s fearful
and dangerous. This is intrinsic authentic to a bear or a rattlesnake, or to some
dangerous situation, can be fear or anger corresponding to the fight-or-flight, can be
both. This is how our emotions are responding to pure perception.

One of the things we respond to emotionally when we bring up a memory or a belief is,
we perceive that image of ourselves or that situation, and we respond emotionally to
perceiving that memory or that self-image. Then our emotion is an automatic response
to just perceiving something that’s in our memory. The memory didn’t create it, but our
emotional body responded to us perceiving it, and now we feel the emotion that we
created as a response to perceiving something beautiful or something unpleasant. The
more we believe something that we perceive, say our imagination of how something
turned out or how it’s going to turn out, the stronger is that emotion. Hope this helps in
understanding how emotion is just a sensory feedback to what we perceive. It can be
something we perceive in our imagination as an agreement, a self-image or the
interpretation. Or that perception can be something really of life as it is.

In this process, I want you to really hunt and pay attention to all the words, all the ways
we describe our emotions. Going back to a previous session on ban words, and once you
pay attention to the wording around or the activity around a certain emotion that would
cause us to avoid it, judge it, try and push it away and look at that agreement about
emotion and take it apart, because the problem is not the emotion. We can start taking
that agreement apart and just allow ourselves to be present with, and say “Hey, it’s just
emotion. I’ll let go of my judging about the emotion, because the emotion isn’t the
problem.” It’s just indicating something else. Let’s go look and see what that is. In this
                                                                                                                           5/10

way, you can really hunt and dissolve the judgments that caused the repression of the
emotions that you feel.

There’s one more element that I would like you to be aware of, as you create a new
understanding of your emotions. There’s something we create either as a by-product of
perceiving something in our imagination, or as a by-product to perceiving something in
life. They are our creations. They are our creations that once we created it, we then
perceive that emotion that we create. We create it, we express it, it comes out of us, and
then we feel that emotion that we just created. As we heighten our awareness of this
dynamic, I’d like this to filter down into your language and the way you describe
emotions and your experience with emotions.

Specifically the big distortion to pay attention to is, anytime we say something to the
effect I’m so happy, I’m angry, I’m guilty, we need to be more precise, because if we go
back to earlier sessions, we talked about the power of words. We’re not anger. We’re or
not guilt. We’re not happiness. Those are our creations and we certainly aren’t our
creations. It gives our mind a distorted image of what we are. We lose our self in that
mis-identity, because guilt, or anger, happiness, is just an emotion, which is just one
aspect of what we’re experiencing in that moment. Guilt that we feel, or anger that we
feel, isn’t what we are.

We need to dispense with phrasing our relationship to our emotions as “I’m so angry” or
“I’m so jealous.” What we can say more accurately is that “I’m experiencing this
emotion of anger”, “I’m experiencing this emotion of jealousy” or “I’m creating this
experience of anger or jealousy.” Just by shifting these words, we are adopting a
different point of view that puts us out of the dream and the energetic force that
emotions take us into. It puts us more in the state of consciousness, awareness, and
more specifically choice. We can decide if we want to act on that emotion that we’re
experiencing or not. If we are the emotion, if we claim in our mind and believe that we
are that emotion, then we have very little choice in what we do, other than what that
emotion would have us do.

But once we shift outside, which we can do, or start to do just by shifting a language to
“I’m experiencing this emotion. This emotion is what I’m feeling.” We are adopting
more of a place of choice as the observer of the emotion, instead of being swept away by
the emotion. This changes our relationship to the emotion, and we are more and more
in a place of power and choice, and less and less in the reaction of what the emotion
would carry us to do. This will help and facilitate refraining from reacting with emotion,
and at the same time allow us to not have to repress them. Because the challenge with
emotion is to allow ourselves to experience them, to be present with them, but to do so
for a place of, and this is particularly with the unpleasant emotions, to do it from a state
of awareness and a place of choice, where we do not have to react in the direction that
that emotion would have us be drawn to, or tempt us to. Then we need to clean up our
language. This will help us adopt a new point of view to be an observer, to be in more in




                                                                                                                           6/10

a powerful place of choice over whether we act on that emotion, or we can refrain.
While we refrain from acting on it we can still be present with the emotions that we’re
feeling.

What we want to do in this assignment for the coming weeks is to become aware of our
emotions as this feedback mechanism. Just the same way you want to notice what your
body temperature is, to tell you whether it’s healthy or unhealthy, we’re going to
monitor our emotions to give us feedback, as to whether emotionally we’re doing
something pleasant or unpleasant. What I’d like you to do is create a chart. A daily chart
of your emotions. I want you to create two sectors, one is for the pleasant emotions you
feel, and one is for the unpleasant emotions you feel. You can create this chart in a
number of ways, but by a minimum of every hour, and preferably every 20 to 30
minutes. Take a moment to look at that previous time interval of 20, 30, or 60 minutes,
and look at what was the most pleasant emotion you experienced. Write down what it
is. For that same time interval, write down what was the most unpleasant emotion
during that time interval, 20, 30, 60 minutes.

Give it a magnitude rating. Say 0-10. If you were laughing with your friends and you felt
all that joy from laughing in the past half hour, maybe that’s an 8. From 0-10, the
intensity was an 8. During that same interval time what was the most unpleasant
emotion that you experienced? Did you get angry? Did you feel guilty? Were you sad at
something somebody said? You got a magnitude range from 0-10. I want you to be
aware of what emotions you’re feeling during that time interval, and the magnitude of
those emotions.

Sometimes our emotions are a little hidden and tough to ferret out. Putting our
attention on these emotions this way will give us a higher acuity and clarity for what’s
going on with us emotionally. It will allow us to hold down the stories that are
happening, and the agreements that are happening. Often when you feel emotions, I
know this happened for me when I started out, I just felt lousy. Something happened,
and I just felt lousy. People ask me “How do you feel?” I said “I feel miserable.” Why?
What else was going on? I said “I don’t know. I just feel this way.” The myriad of stories
that we can have going on is, somebody said something and I felt hurt. That was very
sad about what I was. But that wasn’t all I felt. I also got angry at someone else for
saying that. In my mind I wasn’t allowed or supposed to be angry, so I saw myself get
angry, said I shouldn’t be this way, and I judged myself for being angry. I felt guilty for
being angry.

Perhaps I had a history of being angry where I said “Gosh, I really wish I didn’t get
upset. I shouldn’t do that. I don’t want to get angry anymore.” I made that commitment
to myself, and there it was. I broke that commitment, and now I was frustrated because
I tried to change this dynamic of getting angry, and I wasn’t able to do it. Now, I have
sadness, I’ve got anger, I’ve got guilt and I’ve got frustration. I have them all at once. I
have them from 4 different stories. They’re all sitting in my gut like some giant knot, as
if I swallowed a bowling ball and I don’t feel like eating. I just feel miserable. That’s the
only word I have for it. Lousy and miserable. But what I missed was, there’s 4 different
                                                                                                                           7/10

stories going on with four different lies, and each one has its own emotion.

It took me a while to practice being aware of my emotions, to find the acuity, so that I
could find all 4, and I could look at 4 different stories. When I could find 4 different
emotions, I could find 4 different stories. I can look at each one of those stories
individually and find a way not to believe them. Find some of its faulty logic, then have
it fall apart right in front of me. Those reactions are very difficult to resolve and
dissolve, when they just come as a package called “miserable” or “lousy” and you can’t
get it open. But if we can pull them apart, all those agreements can be dissolved. Seeing
the emotions behind them will help make that a whole lot easier. This is one of the
effects of doing this exercise. When you can have a reaction, and it has 4 or 5 different
emotion, and you have the acuity to know what those different emotions are, you can
see the different agreements, and we can dissolve the different agreements.

What I find interesting as a gender difference, between men and women in this area of
emotions, and this is my experience, that men have repressed our emotions starting in
grade school. It wasn’t okay to feel, there were a lot of emotions you just weren’t going
to feel. For men, this exercise can be challenging, because we’re not used to noticing
what we’re feeling emotionally. A lot of times they’ll be neutral or there’ll be none.
That’s okay. They are behind a door that we closed. Just the fact that we start to look, we
will start to open that door wider and wider, to proceed what we’re feeling emotionally.

Now on the side of women, women are much more aware of what they feel emotionally.
Their conditioning hasn’t been to repress them as much. However what I find
sometimes with women is, women are more inclined to feel that emotion, and then use
that emotion as evidence to whatever the story is as being true. If she feels like this
person doesn’t like her, that feeling that she’s not liked, she uses as evidence to say “Oh,
no. I know she doesn’t like me.” How do you know? “I can feel it.” What she’s feeling is
the result of believing her own story.

Something to realize though, if we have the perception that someone doesn’t like us, and
even if we realize that we are creating the emotion by our own agreement, say perhaps
something embedded in there that says we’re not likable. Even if we say “I’m the one
creating the emotion”, doesn’t mean they don’t like us. It doesn’t mean they like us. It’s
completely independent. We’re creating the emotion, and what they’re doing is
independent of that. We haven’t deduced clearly from this exercise that they like us or
not. That’s a completely separate assessment and you might have to ask them for that.
Of course, they still might not be honest with you. So why worry about it at all?

Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is create a chart. Some kind of daily
journal of what is going on emotionally, or at a minimum every hour. Preferably every
20-30 minutes. If you missed some blocks, go back and fill in those segments of time as
best you can. Put down what that emotion is, try and be as specific as possible. The
emotions we feel, they fall into two categories, they’re unpleasant or they’re pleasant.
The second part is we want to look at the intensity. We want to consider giving it a
value, say 0-10. 0 being pretty neutral, not having any feelings in that direction during
                                                                                                                           8/10

that time period. Or 10 being as high as you go. This charting is just a mechanism to
reinforce what we want to do with our attention, which is to notice what we’re feeling.
Something that I want you to notice while doing this process and why charting will help
is, you’ll notice that all your emotions are temporary. They don’t last.

There’s a great line from the movie Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. There’s two
wonderful lovers that have this great passion for each other, but that they don’t act
upon. Because of the cultural situation it’s not appropriate. One of their mentors says to
them “Even the greatest warriors become cowards when it comes to their emotions.”
Emotions are some of the most frightening things that we experience, because we so
often get overwhelmed and feel like we lose control to them. The truth is, it feels that
way but isn’t that way. We feel like our emotions overwhelm us because that is what we
believe. That confirms the story. We use that fear of our emotions and that
overwhelming power of emotions to believe the story that our emotions can overwhelm
us. But after whatever emotional experience has done, we’re still there. Our emotions
are gone. Each time it proves that our emotions didn’t overwhelm us.

Don’t use that story that our emotions will overwhelm us to be afraid. Sometimes they
take us for a ride, but it’s not really the emotions that take us for a ride. They’re not the
problem. It’s the story that we believe so powerfully, that takes us into the emotion.
That’s the issue. The emotion is just what we experience, because we bought into the
story so completely. When you start to get this awareness, and you start practicing
creating emotions and dissolving them, you will become more and more aware that the
emotions aren’t something to be afraid of. They’re just indicators of what stories that
you bought into. As you practice this exercise, it will become clearer and clearer to you,
that you’re the creator of these emotions. As creator you can dissolve also them. The
way to change your emotions is not to repress them, push them down, or try to get rid of
them. The way to change them is to look at the story, those splinters in our mind that
aren’t true. Pluck them out and see them as the lies they are.

Some people say that the truth hurts. That’s not true. What happens is, when the truth
comes, we see that splinter there. The real truth will tell us that splinter is not true, that
lie right there is not true. In that moment, we’re pulling that splinter out. We’re taking
that lie out of our mind, that story, and we’re like “Gosh that isn’t true at all.” Now when
we take that lie out, we expose it. We cut it out. That’s painful. The same thing as if we
pull the splinter out, it would be painful. But it’s more painful to let it sit in there. The
truth doesn’t hurt. Cutting out the lie, that’s painful. But leaving that lie sit, and create
more pain and more pain and more pain, over who knows how many days and years,
that’s really painful. The truth is the least painful. You just go in once, you cut it out and
you’re done. Continuing to believe in lies and those illusions, that’s really painful. Christ
said the words “You shall know the truth and the truth shall set you free.” My mentor
helped me understand that. Seeing all those stories as not being true, so that we can no

09 Emotions

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/j7DWsS4uQJE

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Emotions lesson audio and the Releasing Emotions audio.
You may want to listen more than once.

2. Practice releasing the emotions with your attention and your breath. You
find it in the second audio above. Do this throughout the day whenever you notice some
emotions. Particularly practice this with small emotions as they show up. This will help
develop the skills, attention, awareness, and confidence so that you will be more
effective when bigger emotions show up later.

3. Journal about what emotions you feel during the day. You can do this using
a tracking app, phone, or journal. This tracking is training your attention to notice your
emotions and to work with them directly. You are bringing your whole body and
nervous system into the process instead of just your thinking mind.

Some notes

The practices have two parts. The first is the awareness of noticing your emotions. This
is the first audio. The second is the “what you do with them” when you notice them.
This is the Releasing Emotions audio.

For the building awareness part:

Because we have been conditioned to repress, or not pay attention to our emotions, we
often over ride being present with them by getting busy with other things. One of them
is to keep our attention in our thoughts, and not notice what our body is feeling. The
noticing part of the practice is designed to build the muscle of moving your attention to




                                                                                                                                   1/5

your feelings in your body. Just having your attention there for some people will be a
new thing. You will have to exercise your attention muscle to focus in a new way. This
might be an effort if you have developed a lot of unconscious habits to avoid feelings.

A critical step in both of these practices is that you are the observer of these emotions.
Refrain from sliding into the perspective of the emotions. If you do you will be in the
perspective of the characters that are expressing the anger, fear, jealousy, insecurity,
etc. If you slide into these character perspectives it will seem like everything they say
and believe is true. From that perspective you will be creating more of the same
emotions instead of letting them go. So attention and perspective are important
elements in this process to maintain.

The process of naming the emotion requires you to keep your attention on that emotion
for more than an instant. It also trains your mind that these feelings are important and
that paying attention to them is valuable. Some people will need to break the habit of
dismissing their emotions quickly. This might look like someone asking how are you.
The response is, “I”m fine,” when there are actually several feelings going on. Or,
noticing that you are stressed or frustrated, but then quickly deciding, “I’ll go for a run,
work out, (get a drink with friends, or play some video games), and then I’ll be over it.”
These are ways to suppress and avoid dealing with uncomfortable emotions. The
problem with these dismissal patterns is that they have long term effects. You haven’t
dealt with the real cause and so patterns persist. You drink more, eat more, work out
more, play more video games, more and more until your life is out of balance. Or
emotions build up into a larger volume and explode in a way that is out of proportion
later. Somebody close to us pays an emotional price. Then later, they pay us back with
an emotional price.

Learning to work through feeling small emotions in a healthy and releasing way will
build the skills to work through the larger emotions when they show up later.

These are two lists of emotions you may find useful as reference. They can be
used to identify what emotions you are feeling. Use whatever references are helpful.

Releasing Emotions Practice

The questions to ask yourself in the audio are about size and intensity of the emotion.
One of the benefits of these questions is that it gives your mind something to think
about, and a way to connect with the emotions as an observer. You could also ask
yourself about the shape, color, weight, or any other property.

By doing this you are training your attention, and mind, to take an interest, notice
sensations, and pick up on nuance of feelings. This engagement helps you to be more
comfortable with what is going on. If you can develop a curiosity about these sensations,
even better. It will help you explore these feelings. The goal of all of this is to help you to





                                                                                                                                   2/5

be more comfortable by being more familiar with what is going on in the present
moment with what you feel. By being more comfortable you can relax your body and
will be able to move the emotions more easily.

The emotions will change in your body as you release them. Paying attention to the
subtle changes and shifts will build confidence that they are moving.

Resistance to change

Fears might sound like: “If I open up to feel some of these emotions I feel like I will
drown in them, or they will never stop. With thoughts like that there is a fear of
overwhelm. I think we have all faced that feeling at some point.

“If I really get in touch with that anger, I don’t know what I will do.” We fear
connecting and feeling any anger because we might lose control.

Notice that in both of these cases there is a fear of feeling an emotion. This is an
emotion about another emotion. (Fear of feeling anger.) When this is the case, it can be
helpful to start noticing the multiple layers of emotions. Cognitively map these layers
helps get past some confusion about what is happening. After mapping these layers, you
can decide which parts you are going to work on releasing, and how much.

By all means break down all this emotional processing work into manageable steps. If
you believe that you will get overwhelmed with a certain emotion, then don’t start there.
Build your confidence with other emotions. Then take on a small part of the anger, grief,
or sadness, etc, in a way that you can remain present.

You don’t have to take on all your big emotions in the first week. Start with breathing
and releasing the small emotions. Build some skills with your attention so that you can
stay present and focused while you release emotions. Get your self comfortable with the
process before moving on to the bigger emotions that appear overwhelming.

At the same time, do some writing about the thoughts “I feel I will get overwhelmed.” or
“I don’t know what I will do”. What emotions are layered into that thought? What
character, or characters are saying these things? Journal about the characters and what
they say and feel about feeling emotions. What assumptions and supporting arguments
do they make about their stories?

They have had a strategy for a long time, probably since you started repressing
emotions at age 4-6. It worked for a number of decades, or so they believe. They believe
that those strategies will still work. As long as they believe these strategies, they will
resist anything new. The more you write about the characters resistance, the more you
will see the limited virtual world they live in. You will also be separating your identity
from them so you can see things more clearly.

It is usually the case that a character is afraid that “The victim is afraid it will get
overwhelmed if it feels ______ emotion” It may help to switch the point of view and
                                                                                                                                   3/5

look at these resistance stories as characters.

At some point, you may see that it is the characters who are afraid of feeling emotions,
and that you can be fine with them. At that point you may find it helpful to help the
characters let go of their fear of feeling emotions with the Releasing breath work.

Common questions

What if I don't know what to name the emotion?
That’s fine. This is a new skill of emotional intelligence you are learning. Given the
number of ways for neural pathways to fire, you can experience thousands of emotions.
You won’t have a name for all of them. Give it your best guess and you will get better at
it over time.

You also might print out an emotion wheel like this one to help guide you.

What are some tracking apps to use with my phone?
I don’t have a personal recommendation to any of these. They are apps that users have
used, found helpful, and recommended back to me.

You may find some are too simple, or others have too many fields to track and are not
simple enough. There’s not a right or wrong way to do it. (see,,, banned words don’t
work for describing this). It’s a matter of finding what works best for you personally.
Moodkit

Universe of Emotions

Daylio – Journal

What if during the releasing work the emotions keep changing?
This is very common, and can be a good thing. There are two approaches. Sometimes
you are letting go of an emotion like anger in your belly. Then you notice that your
throat tightens with fear. This might signify that there is a fear of feeling angry. I
generally recommend that you work on the top layer first. In this case, the fear of
feeling, or connecting with the anger is preventing getting connected with it. So the fear
is the top layer of emotion that you work on first.

At other times, you may find the mind jumping around all over the place. In this
scenario it may mean that your nervous system is uncomfortable and pushing your
attention away from releasing the emotion. At other times you might just have 3 or 4
emotions you are feeling at one time and the mind doesn’t know what to pay attention
to. Pick one, do your best with it, and then move on to another. You might go a couple
rounds with them.

In this scenario you may want to check in with your body, do some acceptance work and
relax. When you are more relaxed in your body you will feel safer, and can release
emotions again.
                                                                                                                                   4/5

What if I don't know what the emotion is by name?
Not knowing the name of the emotions is totally fine. Naming them can be helpful, but
not required. If you can consider that emotions are combinations of neural pathways
firing, context of your imagination, glands secreting, and your nervous system
responding, then you can have an infinite number of emotions. You can’t name them
all. You can also have a feeling that is a combination of 6 different ones.

It’s okay to just say this feels “heavy”, or “tight”.

Regardless of what emotion, and not being able to identify them, you can still do the
releasing breath work process. That’s really the important thing.

If you find your mind getting fixated on naming them, then do some writing about what
character is fixated on that step. This will help you detach from that thought and see it
as just a belief of a character.

Supporting videos


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/tZXmtXDzGto

What you feel even if it is suffering, can be defended with false beliefs

There are often stories of justification defending letting go of emotions. Sometimes you
just have to set your mind with resolve that your emotions will change, and trust that
future self will figure out a way. Not all answers are known when we want them.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/2z6V1y-rmoQ

Change your language and you change your relationship to emotions

One of the changes to make, is to change how you talk about emotions. Be aware, and
articulate with words a proper relationship with emotions. You feel emotions of anger.
You are never angry, sad, or afraid. Those are emotions you feel, not things you are.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/ps7DM7iDyZI

How you feel is not a good measure of progress

Finding big lies, or opening up strong repressed emotions to be released can be
unpleasant. However, that is how healing and change can happen the fastest.
Sometimes the splinter hurts the most as it is being pulled out.
